facts.fact: The English qualifying paper has 10 items totalling 150 marks.
Item 01 essay: 200-250 words, one topic from a list of five, 20 marks.
The essay may be descriptive, analytical, philosophical or based on current affairs.
Item 02 formal letter: ~100 words, 10 marks.
Letter topics: daily office matters, an office problem, or an opinion sought by a ranked officer.
Item 03 press release/appeal: ~100 words, 10 marks.
Press release/appeal topics: a recent concern, problem, disaster or rumours.
Item 04 report: ~150 words, 15 marks, on a function, event, field trip or survey.
Item 05 visual information: ~150 words, 15 marks, on a graph, image, flow chart, table or statistics.
Item 06 formal speech: ~150 words, 15 marks, for an inauguration, seminar or ceremony.
Item 09 grammar MCQs carry 20 marks and come from 14 named areas.
Administrative glossary is one of the 14 syllabus grammar areas.
English has 12 tense forms: 3 times × 4 aspects.
"Since + point" and "for + period" take the present perfect.
already / yet / just / ever signal the present perfect.
yesterday / ago / last year take the simple past, never the present perfect.
"By the time" + past → past perfect (the train had left by the time we arrived).
Stative verbs (know, believe, love, belong) are not used in the continuous.
An action finished before another past action takes the past perfect.
First conditional: if + present, will + verb.
Second conditional: if + past (were), would + verb — unreal present.
Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + V3 — unreal past.
"If I were you" — "were" for all persons in the unreal condition.
"It is high time" is followed by the past tense.
"Lest" takes "should".
"Unless" means "if not", so no extra "not".
No future tense after when/if in a time clause ("when he comes").
Passive = correct form of "be" + past participle, keeping the tense.
Modal passive: must write → must be written.
Continuous passive: is writing → is being written.
"Open the door" → "Let the door be opened".
"Who wrote this?" → "By whom was this written?"
Intransitive verbs (sleep, go, arrive) have no passive.
Some passives take a preposition other than "by": known to, pleased with, surprised at.
Reported speech back-shifts: will → would, can → could, is → was.
tomorrow → the next day; now → then; here → there.
Reported questions use "asked" + wh-/if-whether with statement word order.
A present reporting verb ("says") causes no tense change.
A universal truth keeps its tense in reported speech.
yesterday → the previous day; last night → the previous night; ago → before.
must → had to; shall → should in reported speech.
Commands → told/ordered/requested + to-infinitive; negative → not to.
"Let's" → suggested that … should.
Exclamations → exclaimed with joy/sorrow.
SON 1-2-3: first person follows the Subject, second the Object, third does not change.
"Told" needs a listener (She told me that …); "said to" keeps the listener.
"Too … to" = "so … that … cannot".
"No sooner … than"; "Hardly … when" (never "No sooner … when").
A simple sentence has one finite verb.
A compound sentence joins main clauses with and/but/or/so.
A complex sentence has a main clause + a subordinate clause (because, when, although).
"The largest" = "larger than any other" = "No other … as large as".
"Only he can do it" → "None but he can do it".
"He always comes on time" → "He never fails to come on time".
"Who does not love his country?" → "Everyone loves his country."
"What a beautiful day!" → "It is a very beautiful day."
"One of the + plural" takes a singular verb.
each / every / either / neither (alone) take a singular verb.
With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
"The number of" → singular; "a number of" → plural.
"As well as / along with" → verb agrees with the first subject.
news / mathematics take a singular verb; scissors / trousers / spectacles take plural.
A collective noun acting as one unit (jury, committee) takes a singular verb.
Choose a/an by sound: an hour, a university, an MP.
"The" is used with rivers, seas, oceans, mountain ranges and deserts.
"The" is used with unique things, superlatives and ordinals.
"The" is used with musical instruments, newspapers and holy books.
"The" + adjective = a whole class (the rich, the poor).
A single mountain takes no article (Mount Everest).
No article with languages, meals and games (Telugu, lunch, cricket).
Most countries take no article, but the USA, the UK and the Netherlands do.
few = hardly any (negative); a few = some (positive).
little = hardly any; a little = some (uncountable).
fewer / many for countable nouns; less / much for uncountable.
each = one by one (two or more); every = all (three or more).
accused of; charged with; married to; good at; different from.
at + clock time; on + day/date; in + month/year/season.
between two; among more than two.
beside = next to; besides = in addition to.
by + agent; with + instrument.
die of a disease; die from a cause.
angry with a person; angry at a thing.
deal in = trade; deal with = handle.
abide by; comply with.
conducive to.
insist on.
refrain from.
rely on; independent of.
superior / inferior / senior / junior / prior / preferable + to, never than.
prefer A to B.
congratulate on.
call off = cancel; put off = postpone.
carry out = perform; look into = investigate; give up = stop.
turn down = reject.
put up with = tolerate.
take after = resemble a parent.
run out of = have none left.
come across = find by chance.
set up = establish; give in = surrender.
make up for = compensate.
"Look forward to" takes the -ing form.
bring up = raise a child / mention; look after = take care of.
burn the midnight oil = work late into the night.
bury the hatchet = make peace; at the eleventh hour = at the last moment.
a bolt from the blue = a complete surprise.
beat about the bush = avoid the main point.
hit the nail on the head = say exactly the right thing.
a white elephant = a costly, useless possession.
red tape = excessive official formality.
cry over spilt milk = regret what cannot be undone.
a feather in one's cap = an achievement to be proud of.
once in a blue moon = very rarely.
spill the beans = reveal a secret.
break the ice = start a conversation.
at loggerheads = in strong disagreement.
Achilles' heel = a weak point.
a red-letter day = a memorable, happy day.
in hot water = in trouble.
bureaucracy = government by officials.
aviary = place for birds; polyglot = knows many languages; illiterate = cannot read or write.
autocracy = rule by one person with absolute power.
anarchy = absence of government.
plutocracy = rule by the wealthy.
theocracy = rule by religious leaders.
omniscient = all-knowing (vs omnipotent all-powerful, omnipresent everywhere).
philanthropist = lover of mankind; misanthrope = hater of mankind.
bibliophile = lover of books.
insolvent = unable to pay debts.
posthumous = born or published after the father's or author's death.
unanimous = with everyone agreeing.
pandemic = a disease spreading over a whole country or the world.
pseudonym = a false name used by an author.
illegible = cannot be read; edible = fit to be eaten.
extempore = spoken without preparation.
panacea = a remedy for all ills.
mortuary = place where dead bodies are kept; granary = for grain; apiary = for bees.
regicide = killing of one's king.
benevolent = kind (antonym malevolent).
candid = frank (antonym evasive).
abundant = plentiful (antonym scarce).
obstinate = stubborn (antonym flexible).
transparent = clear (antonym opaque).
diligent = hard-working (antonym lazy).
frugal = thrifty (antonym extravagant).
agenda = items to be discussed; minutes = the record made after a meeting.
quorum = the minimum number of members needed for a meeting.
memorandum = a note setting out terms or information.
ad hoc = for a particular purpose only, temporary.
ex officio = by virtue of one's office.
bona fide = genuine, in good faith.
sine die = without fixing a date.
suo motu = on its own motion, without a petition.
ultra vires = beyond one's legal powers.
prima facie = at first sight.
pro rata = in proportion.
status quo = the existing state of affairs.
in camera = in private, not in open court.
de facto = in fact; de jure = by law.
ex gratia = as a favour, not as a legal duty.
inter alia = among other things.
sub judice = under judicial consideration.
ordinance = a law made by the executive when the legislature is not in session.
affidavit = a written statement on oath.
circular = an order sent to many offices at once.
affect (verb) vs effect (noun).
stationary = still; stationery = paper and pens.
principal = head / main; principle = rule.
complement = completes; compliment = praise.
council = a body; counsel = advice or a lawyer.
accept = receive; except = leave out.
loose = not tight; lose = misplace.
eminent = distinguished; imminent = about to happen.
elicit = draw out; illicit = illegal.
adverse = unfavourable; averse = unwilling.
canvas = cloth; canvass = seek votes.
discreet = careful; discrete = separate.
personal = private; personnel = staff.
precede = come before; proceed = go on.
ensure = make certain; insure = protect by insurance.
Negative in- becomes il- before l, ir- before r, im- before m/p.
-less = without; -ful = full of.
Prefixes un-, dis-, mis-, non-, anti-, pre-, post-, re- change a word's meaning.
-ness/-ment/-tion make nouns; -ize makes verbs; -ly makes adverbs.
Contrast = however/but/yet/nevertheless; addition = moreover/furthermore; result = therefore/hence.
Similarity = similarly / likewise.
Condition linkers: unless, provided that, in case.
Concession linkers: although, even though, despite.
Cause linkers: because, since, as, owing to.
Purpose linkers: so that, in order to.
"Despite" takes no "of"; "in spite of" does.
Formal letter layout: address, date, receiver, Subject, salutation, purpose → details → request, close.
Dear Sir/Madam → Yours faithfully.
A letter to a named person (Dear Mr Rao) closes Yours sincerely.
Letter tone: polite, formal, no contractions, purpose in the first line.
A press release opens with FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE, a headline and a dateline.
A press release follows the inverted pyramid — the most important fact first.
A press release ends with ### or ENDS.
An appeal names the cause and the exact help needed.
A report opens with the 5 Ws and is third person, past tense, objective.
A report carries a heading and a by-line.
Reports often use the passive ("The function was inaugurated by …").
A survey report runs purpose → method → findings → recommendations.
Visual information: describe the main trend and key figures — do not interpret.
A line graph shows a trend over time.
A bar chart compares quantities.
A pie chart shows parts of a whole.
A flow chart shows the stages of a process.
Trend words: rose sharply, declined steadily, peaked, remained stable, fluctuated.
A speech addresses dignitaries in order of rank, then the occasion, points, appeal, thanks.
A welcome address opens a function; a vote of thanks closes it.
